title: Claude Managed Agents and Evolution of Agentic Surfaces — Gagan Bhat & Isabella Kai He, Anthropic

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 97%).

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Claude managed agents is a platform for developers building production agents. The talk is addressed to developers and engineers building agent systems, covering SDK evolution, managed infrastructure, and the developer ownership boundary.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The SRE Investigator agent demo investigates production latency incidents, and field lessons address enterprise security concerns (VPC deployment, credential isolation, self-hosted sandboxes). Enterprise operations teams are a primary audience.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The architectural principles about harness assumptions, brain-hands decoupling, and session durability are broadly applicable across all agent deployment domains, not limited to a specific vertical.

summary: Gagan Bhat and Isabella He from Anthropic's Applied AI team present the evolution of agentic surfaces from the Messages API through the Claude Agent SDK to Claude Managed Agents. The central thesis is that harnesses—software wrapping a model to compensate for its limitations—encode assumptions that go stale as models improve. When Sonnet 4.5 exhibited context anxiety (wrapping up work early near context limits), the team built context resets into the harness; when Opus 4.5 shipped without that behavior, the fix became pure overhead. The foundational architectural decision is decoupling the brain (agent loop) from the hands (tool execution environment), enabling parallel startup (60% faster time-to-first-token at P50, 90%+ at P95), recoverable failures (dead sandboxes retried, dead brains resumed from session logs), and durable session logging. Claude Managed Agents is built on three primitives: agent (model, prompts, tools, skills), environment (sandboxed container with network limits), and session (durable cloud resource logging every interaction). Sessions have four states—idle, running, rescheduling, terminated—enabling reliability. The session log serves triple duty: observability, context recovery (reading slices back into the context window after Claude discards them), and input to dreaming. Four field lessons cover credential isolation via vaults (decrypted only at tool execution, never visible to the model), latency gains from decoupling, session logs as the foundation for observability and memory, and self-hosted sandboxes with MCP tunnels for security-conscious enterprise teams running tool execution within their own VPC. Frontier features include dreaming (a periodic batch process that rewrites agent memory from session transcripts) and outcomes (grader agents that verify task success against user-defined rubrics and iterate until criteria are met). The closing thesis: harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve, and managed agents aims to close the gap between static product surfaces and evolving model capabilities. A demo shows building an SRE Investigator agent from scratch to diagnose a P99 latency spike using the three primitives end-to-end.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk are deeply intertwined: the brain-hands decoupling is simultaneously an infrastructure decision (parallel startup, recoverable failures, credential isolation) and an AI architecture decision (separating the reasoning loop from tool execution). The harness staleness principle bridges model behavior (context anxiety in Sonnet 4.5) with engineering practice (when to remove compensating harness code). The three primitives—agent, environment, session—define both the API surface and the operational model, while the durable session log is simultaneously an observability tool, a context engineering mechanism, and the substrate for dreaming (AI self-improvement). Credential isolation and self-hosted sandboxes are both DevOps practices and AI safety measures. Together, these concepts illustrate that production agent systems require co-design of infrastructure and AI capabilities: the harness is not merely plumbing around a model but a first-class architectural surface that must evolve in lockstep with model capabilities. The talk's evolution narrative (Messages API → Agent SDK → Managed Agents) shows each stage solving infrastructure challenges the previous could not, culminating in a managed platform where the harness itself becomes the product.
temporalContext: The video was published August 11, 2026. Claude Managed Agents launched in public beta on April 8, 2026 — approximately 4 months before the talk. The speakers' companion blog post was published June 10, 2026. Dreaming entered research preview on May 19, 2026. The engineering blog post on brain-hands decoupling was published April 8, 2026. The talk represents Anthropic's managed agent infrastructure state as of mid-2026, with rapid feature additions (outcomes, multi-agent orchestration, dreaming) occurring in the months between product launch and this presentation. The context anxiety behavior was observed in Sonnet 4.5 and resolved with Opus 4.5, both released before the talk.
takeaways: Harnesses encode assumptions about what the model cannot do on its own, and those assumptions go stale as models improve—when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent.
Decoupling the brain (agent loop) from the hands (tool execution) enables parallel startup (60% faster TTFT at P50, 90%+ at P95), recoverable failures, and durable session logging.

Claude managed agents is built around three primitives: agent (definition), environment (container), and session (durable log of all interactions) with four states—idle, running, rescheduling, terminated.
The durable session log does triple duty: observability, context recovery when Claude discards information mid-run, and input to dreaming for memory improvement.

Dreaming runs as a periodic batch process over session transcripts and current memory state, extracting new insights to feed back and edit memory so the next day's agent sessions are automatically more intelligent.
Outcomes uses a separate grader agent that checks task completion against user-defined success rubrics and keeps the agent iterating until criteria are met, unlocking more reliable task completion.

Credentials should be kept in vaults, decrypted only at tool execution runtime, so the model never sees security tokens; self-hosted sandboxes and MCP tunnels let enterprise teams run tool execution within their own VPC.
Harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve; managed agents aims to close the gap between static product surfaces and frontier model capabilities.

concepts.name: Agentic surfaces evolution
concepts.explanation: The three-stage progression from the Messages API (tokens in/out, customers hand-rolled agentic loops) to the Claude Agent SDK (packaged harness with built-in loop, tools, sandboxing) to Claude Managed Agents (fully managed infrastructure handling brain, hands, and all production concerns).
concepts.importance: This evolution frames the entire talk and illustrates how the abstraction level for building agents has risen over three years, with each stage solving infrastructure challenges the previous could not.

concepts.name: Agentic loop
concepts.explanation: The reasoning loop where the model receives input, decides on actions, calls tools, observes results, and iterates until the task is complete. This is the 'brain' in the brain-hands decoupling architecture.
concepts.importance: The agentic loop is the core computational pattern that distinguishes agents from single-call LLM interactions, and its management is what Anthropic takes over in managed agents.

concepts.name: Dreaming
concepts.explanation: A periodic batch process that uses session transcripts and the agent's current memory state as input, extracts new insights and organized structures, and feeds them back to edit memory so that the next day's agent sessions are automatically more intelligent.
concepts.importance: Dreaming is the mechanism for self-improving agents, representing a frontier where agent systems learn from their own execution history without human intervention.

concepts.name: Outcomes (grader agents)
concepts.explanation: A feature where a separate grader agent runs alongside the agent loop, checking whether the agent accomplished the task against user-defined success rubrics including failure cases. If the grader determines the task is incomplete, the agent keeps trying until criteria are met.
concepts.importance: Outcomes moves agents toward understanding what success means and having a mechanism to iterate, increasing reliability and unlocking tasks not previously possible.

concepts.name: Context anxiety in LLMs
concepts.explanation: A model behavior exhibited by Sonnet 4.5 where the model wraps up work early when approaching context limits, even when more work remains. This prompted harness-level context resets that became pure overhead when Opus 4.5 shipped without the behavior.
concepts.importance: Context anxiety is a concrete example of model-specific behaviors that harnesses compensate for, and its disappearance illustrates the harness staleness problem in practice.

concepts.name: Self-improving agents
concepts.explanation: Agents that become more intelligent over time through dreaming, where periodic batch processes extract insights from past sessions and update memory so subsequent runs benefit from accumulated experience.
concepts.importance: Self-improvement represents the frontier of agent capability, moving from static agents that perform the same each run to systems that learn and adapt from their own history.

concepts.name: Organizational memory
concepts.explanation: An emerging memory system at organizational scale that stores team runbooks and details, complementing individual memory (user-specific) and dreaming (self-improvement) as part of a unified memory architecture.
concepts.importance: Organizational memory extends agent intelligence beyond individual sessions and users, enabling team-level knowledge accumulation and reuse.

concepts.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration
concepts.explanation: MCP is used to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP tunnels let enterprise teams expose MCP servers to agents without running them over the public internet, keeping servers in private networks with only outbound calls to the agent loop.
concepts.importance: MCP integration is the standard mechanism for extending agent capabilities with external tools, and MCP tunnels are critical for secure enterprise deployment.

concepts.name: Harnesses as limiting factor
concepts.explanation: The closing thesis that as models evolve on an exponential trajectory, harnesses have become the limiting factor to what models can achieve. Managed agents aims to close the gap between static product surfaces and frontier model capabilities.
concepts.importance: This reframes the engineering challenge: the bottleneck is no longer model capability but the infrastructure wrapping it, motivating the managed agents approach.

concepts.name: Context window management
concepts.explanation: The practice of managing what information is in the model's context window at any given time, including discarding and recovering context. In managed agents, the context window is separated from the session, enabling strategic context engineering.
concepts.importance: Effective context window management is what separates production-ready agents from prototypes, and the session log makes it recoverable rather than destructive.

concepts.name: Brain-hands decoupling
concepts.explanation: The foundational architectural decision to separate the agent loop (brain) from the tool execution environment (hands). Initially co-located in one container, the split enables parallel startup, recoverable failures, and durable session logging.
concepts.importance: This is the core architectural principle of Claude Managed Agents, enabling all downstream benefits including latency reduction, fault tolerance, and security isolation.

concepts.name: Harness staleness principle
concepts.explanation: Harnesses encode assumptions about what the model cannot do on its own. These assumptions go stale as models improve—when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent. Sonnet 4.5's context anxiety fix became dead weight when Opus 4.5 shipped without the behavior.
concepts.importance: This principle explains why static harnesses become the limiting factor for agent performance and motivates the managed agents approach of keeping infrastructure swappable and agile.

concepts.name: Three architectural primitives (agent, environment, session)
concepts.explanation: Claude Managed Agents is built around three independent, swappable primitives: the agent (model, prompts, tools, skills), the environment (container with network limits), and the session (durable cloud resource persisting every interaction).
concepts.importance: These primitives define both the API surface and the operational model, enabling composable agent construction and clear ownership boundaries between developer and platform.

concepts.name: Durable session log
concepts.explanation: A durable cloud resource that logs every interaction during agent execution—user messages, model responses, tool executions, and results—written as a play-by-play event stream.
concepts.importance: The session log is the backbone of observability, context recovery, and memory improvement, serving triple duty as the substrate for three different operational concerns.

concepts.name: Context recovery from session logs
concepts.explanation: In traditional harnesses the context window and session are one and the same, so discarded context cannot be recovered. In managed agents, the harness can read slices of context from the durable session log back into the context window after Claude discards information mid-run.
concepts.importance: This separates effective agents from those lost in context rot, enabling long-running sessions that maintain continuity across context window boundaries.

concepts.name: Credential isolation via vaults
concepts.explanation: Security credentials are stored in vaults and decrypted only at tool execution runtime, so the model never sees security tokens. Brain-hands separation facilitates this by keeping the reasoning loop isolated from the execution environment.
concepts.importance: This is a critical production security pattern for agentic systems, preventing credential leakage through model outputs or prompt injection.

concepts.name: Self-hosted sandboxes and MCP tunnels
concepts.explanation: Because the brain is decoupled from the hands, the hands can run anywhere including in a customer's VPC. Self-hosted sandboxes let customers control their sandbox control plane, and MCP tunnels expose MCP servers to agents without running them over the public internet—servers stay in private networks making only outbound calls.
concepts.importance: This enables security-conscious enterprise teams to adopt managed agents while keeping tool execution and data within their own infrastructure and policies.

concepts.name: Recoverable failure patterns
concepts.explanation: Decoupling brain from hands turns failure into something recoverable: if the sandbox dies, the brain spins up a new one and retries; if the brain dies, it resumes from the durable session log.
concepts.importance: This is the reliability foundation for long-running agents that must operate for hours or days without manual intervention.

concepts.name: Observability via session event logging
concepts.explanation: The session log contains events of everything that happens during agent execution, surfaced in a UI to provide full observability including event traces, tool usage, and play-by-play execution records.
concepts.importance: Observability is essential for debugging, auditing, and trusting production agent systems, and the session log makes it a built-in capability rather than an add-on.

concepts.name: Parallel startup optimization
concepts.explanation: In the old single-container design, the model could not start reasoning until container setup finished. With decoupling, model reasoning starts immediately while container setup runs in parallel, and setup can be skipped entirely if unneeded. Measured at 60% faster time-to-first-token at P50 and over 90% improvement at P95.
concepts.importance: This quantified latency improvement is a key engineering benefit of the brain-hands split, directly impacting user experience and cost.

concepts.name: Four session states
concepts.explanation: Sessions have four states—idle, running, rescheduling, and terminated—enabling the agent to always resume an existing session and providing a state machine for production reliability and recovery.
concepts.importance: The session state machine is the operational backbone for managing agent lifecycle, enabling pause/resume, retry, and clean termination in production.

concepts.name: Context engineering (separating context window from session)
concepts.explanation: Context engineering separates effective agents from those lost in context rot. The key insight is decoupling the ephemeral context window from the durable session, so that context can be strategically managed, recovered, and curated rather than being lost when the model discards it.
concepts.importance: This is a first-class engineering discipline for production agents, distinct from prompt engineering, that determines whether long-running agents maintain coherence over time.

sections.title: Introduction and plan
sections.summary: Gagan and Isabella introduce themselves as members of Anthropic's Applied AI team, situated at the intersection of product, research, and go-to-market. They outline the session: evolution of agentic surfaces, engineering principles behind Claude managed agents, a demo, field lessons, and building at the frontier.

sections.title: Evolution of agentic surfaces
sections.summary: AI progress is accelerating, and task complexity has grown from simple Q&A to delegating tasks to agents owning entire outcomes. The Messages API (launched with Claude 3) was tokens in/out. Customers hand-rolled agentic loops to fetch information and manage context, but faced production infrastructure challenges: session management, observability, credentials, hosting, sandboxing, and file system access. The Claude Agent SDK packaged the Claude Code harness with a built-in loop, tools, and sandboxing, but developers still handled credentials and hosting. Claude managed agents takes over everything: brain (agentic loop and Claude), hands (sandbox), plus all infrastructure.

sections.title: Production infrastructure challenges enumerated
sections.summary: Gagan enumerates six challenges as questions: hosting and scaling, session management, file system access, execution isolation, credentials, and observability. These consumed significant team time, motivating Claude managed agents.

sections.title: Harnesses encode assumptions that go stale
sections.summary: Isabella explains the core principle: harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude cannot do on its own. These assumptions must be questioned frequently because they go stale as models improve. Sonnet 4.5 exhibited context anxiety, wrapping up work early near context limits. The team built context resets into the harness. When Opus 4.5 shipped without context anxiety, the fix became pure overhead, adding latency and discarding cache incorrectly. The takeaway: when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent.

sections.title: Designing for tomorrow and long-running agents
sections.summary: Harnesses must be designed for future model capabilities and remain agile. Claude managed agents is built around a small set of independent, swappable primitives. Long-running agents (like Claude Code and Claude Tag) are increasingly asynchronous and need context engineering, secure sandboxes, reliability over hours or days, and workflow parallelization.

sections.title: Decoupling the brain from the hands
sections.summary: The foundational architectural decision is decoupling the brain (agent loop) from the hands (tool execution). Initially both lived in the same container, which was convenient but introduced limitations. The container blocked the agent from starting until setup finished, and either half failing took the whole agent down.

sections.title: Reliability benefits and three core primitives
sections.summary: Decoupling enables recoverable failure: if the sandbox dies, the brain spins up a new one and retries; if the brain dies, it resumes from a durable session log. Claude managed agents is built around three primitives: the agent (model, prompts, tools, skills), the environment (container with network limits), and the session (durable cloud resource persisting every interaction, unlocking observability, long-running execution, and reliability).

sections.title: Session states and context engineering
sections.summary: Sessions have four states: idle, running, rescheduling, and terminated. The agent can always resume an existing session. Context engineering separates effective agents from those lost in context rot. In traditional harnesses the context window and session are one and the same, so discarded context cannot be recovered. In managed agents, everything is logged to a durable session log, so the harness can read slices of context back into the window after Claude discards them. Developers customize context management and domain expertise (prompts, tools, skills), while Anthropic manages the agent loop, memory, and observability.

sections.title: Demo: SRE Investigator agent
sections.summary: Gagan demos building an SRE Investigator agent from scratch to investigate a P99 latency spike. Step one: agent definition with name, model (Opus 4.5), system prompt, standard tools (bash, grep, blob), and MCP toolset connecting to a dashboard. Step two: environment (SRE sandbox with networking limited to allowed MCP server hosts). Step three: upload application logs and skills. Step four: create a session and kick it off. The agent greps logs, pulls metrics via MCP, finds recent deploys, isolates the incident, finds the code diff, and synthesizes a root cause. An observability dashboard shows full event traces, tool usage, and session logs.

sections.title: Field lessons: credentials and latency
sections.summary: Lesson one: keep credentials away from the agent—brain-hands separation helps, and vaults store security credentials decrypted only at tool execution runtime, so the model never sees tokens. Lesson two: decoupling brain from hands significantly improved latency. In the old single-container design, the model couldn't start reasoning until container setup finished. With decoupling, model reasoning starts immediately while container setup runs in parallel, and setup can be skipped entirely if unneeded. Measured results: 60% faster time to first token at P50 and over 90% improvement at P95.

sections.title: Field lesson: session logs as memory
sections.summary: Lesson three: session logs answer two customer questions—how to see what's happening under the hood, and how to make agents better over time. The session log contains every event during execution: user messages, model responses, tool executions, and results, written play-by-play. Surfaced in a UI it provides observability. The same log also improves memory by providing a history of past executions, and combined with dreaming, allows memory to be updated and improved over time so the next agent run is better.

sections.title: Field lesson: self-hosted sandboxes and MCP tunnels
sections.summary: Lesson four: security for tool execution. Security-conscious enterprise teams wanted tool execution controlled within their own VPC. Because the brain is decoupled from the hands, the hands can run anywhere, including in a customer's VPC. Self-hosted sandboxes let customers control their sandbox control plane and run tools under their own policies. MCP tunnels let teams expose MCP servers to agents without running them over the public internet—servers stay in the private network, making only outbound calls to the Claude agent loop.

sections.title: Frontier feature: dreaming
sections.summary: Dreaming uses session transcripts and the agent's current memory state as input to a periodic batch process that extracts new insights and organized structures, feeding them back to edit memory so the next day's agent sessions are automatically more intelligent. This is how self-improving agents work. Dreaming and memory are cornerstones of a new frontier unified memory system: individual memory remembers user-specific things, dreaming enables self-improvement, and a new organizational-scale memory is emerging to store team runbooks and details.

sections.title: Frontier feature: outcomes
sections.summary: Outcomes lets users define success criteria as a rubric, including failure cases. A separate grader agent runs alongside the agent loop, checking whether the agent accomplished the task against the defined rubric. If the grader determines the task is incomplete, the agent keeps trying until it meets the success criteria. This moves toward agents understanding what success means and having a mechanism to iterate, increasing reliability and unlocking tasks not possible months ago as models become more capable.

sections.title: Closing: harnesses as the limiting factor
sections.summary: Managed agents aims to close the gap between what products offer with static harnesses and what models can actually do. As models evolve on an exponential trajectory, harnesses have become the limiting factor. The core architectural foundation plus new features are designed to close that gap, making Claude managed agents a harness that is production-ready for real workloads and structured to capture frontier intelligence as models continue to evolve.

demonstrations: SRE Investigator agent demo: building a production-grade agent from scratch using Claude managed agents to investigate a P99 latency spike, using agent definition (Opus 4.5, bash/grep/MCP tools), environment (sandbox with limited networking), and session primitives; agent greps logs, pulls metrics via MCP, finds deploys and code diffs, and synthesizes root cause
limitations: Same-container approach blocked the agent from starting until setup finished
Stale harnesses can take weeks or months to migrate to a new model
Customer harnesses built around older Claude models are more rigid
Traditional harness implementations conflate context window and session, preventing context recovery after discarding
Static harnesses in products create a gap between what models can do and what surfaces offer

organization.name: Anthropic
organization.summary: Anthropic is an AI safety and research company and Public Benefit Corporation that builds reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. It develops Claude, a family of frontier AI models, and operates the Claude Platform including Claude Managed Agents, a suite of composable APIs for building and deploying cloud-hosted agents at scale. The Agentic Systems team within Anthropic's Platform organization builds and operates Claude Managed Agents. Both speakers (Gagan Bhat and Isabella He) are Members of Technical Staff on Anthropic's Applied AI team, which operates at the intersection of product, research, and go-to-market.
organization.status: Active, independent Public Benefit Corporation. Claude Managed Agents core API is in public beta with managed-agents-2026-04-01 header per official documentation. The Anthropic Help Center lists Claude Managed Agents overall as Research preview, creating a status discrepancy with official documentation.

technologies.label: Claude Managed Agents Platform
technologies.summary: Claude Managed Agents is Anthropic's managed agent platform that decouples the brain (agent loop) from the hands (tool execution), built on three primitives: agent (model, prompts, tools, skills), environment (sandboxed container with network limits), and session (durable cloud resource logging every interaction). Sessions have four states (idle, running, rescheduling, terminated) enabling reliability and recovery. The platform delivers parallel startup (60% faster TTFT at P50, 90%+ at P95), recoverable failures (dead sandboxes retried, dead brains resumed from session logs), context recovery from durable session logs, credential isolation via vaults, self-hosted sandboxes for VPC deployment, and frontier features including dreaming (periodic memory rewriting) and outcomes (grader agents verifying task success). The core thesis is that harnesses encode assumptions about model limitations that go stale as models improve, making managed agents necessary to close the gap between static product surfaces and evolving model capabilities.
technologies.role: Primary subject of the talk—the managed agent platform whose architecture, primitives, field lessons, and frontier features constitute the core content

technologies.label: Claude Agent SDK
technologies.summary: The Claude Agent SDK was the intermediate evolution step between the Messages API and Claude Managed Agents. It packaged the Claude Code harness with a built-in agentic loop, tools, and sandboxing, reducing the infrastructure burden compared to hand-rolling loops. However, developers still had to handle credentials, hosting, and other production concerns themselves, which motivated the move to fully managed agents.
technologies.role: Intermediate step in the three-stage evolution of agentic surfaces (Messages API to Agent SDK to Managed Agents), mentioned as the predecessor that still left developers handling credentials and hosting

technologies.label: Anthropic Messages API
technologies.summary: The Anthropic Messages API was the original tokens-in/tokens-out API launched with Claude 3, representing the starting point of the agentic surfaces evolution. Customers hand-rolled their own agentic loops to fetch information and manage context, but faced significant production infrastructure challenges including session management, observability, credentials, hosting, sandboxing, and file system access. These challenges motivated the evolution toward the Claude Agent SDK and ultimately Claude Managed Agents.
technologies.role: Starting point of the three-stage evolution narrative, representing the lowest abstraction level where customers hand-rolled agentic loops and faced production infrastructure challenges

technologies.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
technologies.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the standard tool integration protocol used within Claude Managed Agents to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP tunnels are a key feature for secure enterprise deployment, letting teams expose MCP servers to agents without running them over the public internet—servers stay in private networks making only outbound calls to the Claude agent loop. This enables security-conscious enterprise teams to adopt managed agents while keeping tool execution and data within their own infrastructure.
technologies.role: Tool integration protocol enabling external tool connections in the SRE Investigator demo, and MCP tunnels discussed as a field lesson for secure enterprise deployment within customer VPCs

evidence.excerpt: harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude cannot do on its own
evidence.supports: Core principle that harness assumptions go stale as models improve

evidence.excerpt: when Opus 4.5 came out... this behavior went away entirely... the fixes that we'd added into the harness itself became dead weight
evidence.supports: Harness fixes for context anxiety became pure overhead with Opus 4.5

evidence.excerpt: when the model moves and the harness doesn't, it degrades the agent
evidence.supports: Stale harness assumptions degrade agent performance

evidence.excerpt: the decision to decouple the brain from the hands of the agent
evidence.supports: Foundational architectural decision to split agent loop from tool execution

evidence.excerpt: the brain could just spin up a new sandbox and retry and then continue as it left off
evidence.supports: Decoupling enables recoverable failure for dead sandboxes

evidence.excerpt: everything that the agent does is logged into a durable session resource in a session log, which means that the brain of the agent can actually just read from that session log
evidence.supports: Session log enables brain recovery and resume after death

evidence.excerpt: the harness can actually just read in slices of that context from the session log into its current window
evidence.supports: Session log enables context recovery after Claude discards information mid-run

evidence.excerpt: 60% faster time to first token for P50 use cases... over 90% improvements in latency for time to first token in P95 use cases
evidence.supports: Quantified latency improvement from brain-hands decoupling

evidence.excerpt: session log essentially contains events of everything that happened during an agent execution
evidence.supports: Session log captures all agent execution events for observability

evidence.excerpt: the hands can run anywhere, including in your virtual private cloud
evidence.supports: Self-hosted sandboxes enable VPC-based tool execution

evidence.excerpt: periodic batch process with what we call dreaming, it allows us to extract new insights and new organized structures
evidence.supports: Dreaming is a periodic batch process that improves agent memory

evidence.excerpt: outcomes essentially starts a separate grader agent that runs alongside your agent loop and looks at whether that agent was actually able to accomplish the task
evidence.supports: Outcomes feature uses grader agents to verify task completion
